'use client';

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import Link from 'next/link';
import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation';

export default function Navigation() {
    const [isDark, setIsDark] = useState(false);
    const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = useState(false);
    const pathname = usePathname();

    useEffect(() => {
        if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
            const savedTheme = localStorage.getItem('theme');
            const prefersDark = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches;

            const shouldBeDark = savedTheme === 'dark' || (!savedTheme && prefersDark);

            setIsDark(shouldBeDark);
            updateTheme(shouldBeDark);

            // Check initial screen size
            const checkScreenSize = () => {
                setIsMobile(window.innerWidth <= 768);
            };

            checkScreenSize();
            window.addEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);

            return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);
        }
    }, []);

    const updateTheme = (dark: boolean) => {
        if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
            const root = document.documentElement;

            if (dark) {
                root.style.setProperty('--bg-primary', '#000000');
                root.style.setProperty('--text-primary', '#ffffff');
                root.style.setProperty('--bg-secondary', '#111111');
                root.style.setProperty('--text-secondary', '#cccccc');
                root.style.setProperty('--border-color', '#333333');
                root.classList.add('dark');
            } else {
                root.style.setProperty('--bg-primary', '#ffffff');
                root.style.setProperty('--text-primary', '#000000');
                root.style.setProperty('--bg-secondary', '#f8f9fa');
                root.style.setProperty('--text-secondary', '#666666');
                root.style.setProperty('--border-color', '#e5e7eb');
                root.classList.remove('dark');
            }
        }
    };

    const toggleTheme = () => {
        const newTheme = !isDark;
        setIsDark(newTheme);
        updateTheme(newTheme);

        if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
            localStorage.setItem('theme', newTheme ? 'dark' : 'light');
        }
    };

    const isActive = (path: string) => {
        if (path === '/' && pathname === '/') return true;
        if (path !== '/' && pathname.startsWith(path)) return true;
        return false;
    };

    return (

**Add: `src/components/LenisScroll.tsx`**

```diff
+'use client';
+
+import { useEffect } from 'react';
+import Lenis from 'lenis';
+
+declare global {
+  interface Window {
+    __lenis?: Lenis;
+  }
+}
+
+export default function LenisScroll() {
+  useEffect(() => {
+    if (typeof window === 'undefined') return;
+
+    const lenis = new Lenis({
+      lerp: 0.1,
+      smoothWheel: true,
+      smoothTouch: false,
+      wheelMultiplier: 1.2,
+    });
+
+    window.__lenis = lenis;
+
+    let frameId: number;
+
+    const raf = (time: number) => {
+      lenis.raf(time);
+      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(raf);
+    };
+
+    frameId = requestAnimationFrame(raf);
+
+    const handleInitialHash = () => {
+      const hash = window.location.hash;
+      if (!hash || !hash.startsWith('#')) return;
+      const target = document.querySelector(hash) as HTMLElement | null;
+      if (!target) return;
+      lenis.scrollTo(target, { immediate: true, offset: -80 });
+    };
+
+    handleInitialHash();
+
+    return () => {
+      cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
+      lenis.destroy();
+      if (window.__lenis === lenis) {
+        delete window.__lenis;
+      }
+    };
+  }, []);
+
+  return null;
+}
+
```

        content: `
# Riverpod: The Future of Flutter State Management

Have you ever felt frustrated trying to manage data in your Flutter app? You're not alone! State management can be one of the trickiest parts of app development, but Riverpod is here to make your life so much easier.

## What Makes Riverpod Special?

Think of Riverpod as your app's personal assistant that never forgets anything and always knows exactly what your app needs at any moment. It's like having a super-organized friend who keeps track of all your app's data and makes sure everything stays in sync.

### Why Developers Love Riverpod

**It Catches Your Mistakes Early**
Remember those annoying bugs that only show up when users are actually using your app? Riverpod helps catch these problems before your app even runs. It's like having a spell-checker but for your code logic.

**No More Context Confusion**
One of the most frustrating things in Flutter development is dealing with context dependencies. Riverpod eliminates this headache completely. You can access your data from anywhere in your app without jumping through hoops.

**Testing Becomes a Breeze**
Testing apps can be tedious, but Riverpod makes it surprisingly enjoyable. You can easily test different scenarios and make sure your app behaves correctly in all situations.

**Memory Management on Autopilot**
Worried about your app using too much memory? Riverpod automatically cleans up resources you're not using anymore. It's like having a personal housekeeper for your app's memory.

## Getting Started is Simple

The beauty of Riverpod is that you can start small and gradually adopt more features as you become comfortable. You don't need to rewrite your entire app overnight.

### Your First Steps

Setting up Riverpod is surprisingly straightforward. You add it to your project, wrap your app with a special widget, and you're ready to go. It's designed to be beginner-friendly while being powerful enough for complex applications.

### Understanding the Basics

Riverpod works with the concept of "providers" - think of them as containers that hold your data and logic. These containers are smart enough to know when to update, when to refresh, and when to clean themselves up.

## Real-World Benefits

**Faster Development**
Once you get the hang of Riverpod, you'll find yourself building features much faster. The clear patterns and helpful tools mean less time debugging and more time creating.

**Better App Performance**
Apps built with Riverpod tend to be more responsive and use resources more efficiently. Your users will notice the difference in how smooth everything feels.

**Easier Collaboration**
If you're working with a team, Riverpod's clear structure makes it easier for everyone to understand and contribute to the codebase. New team members can get up to speed quickly.

## Making the Switch

If you're currently using other state management solutions, don't worry! Riverpod is designed to work alongside existing code. You can migrate gradually, one feature at a time, without breaking anything.

The learning curve is gentler than you might expect. The official documentation is excellent, and the community is incredibly helpful and welcoming to newcomers.

## The Bottom Line

Riverpod isn't just another tool - it's a game-changer that makes Flutter development more enjoyable and productive. Whether you're building your first app or your fiftieth, Riverpod helps you write better code with less stress.

Ready to give it a try? Your future self will thank you for making the switch to this powerful, developer-friendly solution.

+'use client';
+
+import type { MouseEvent } from 'react';
+import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
+import Link from 'next/link';
+import Image from 'next/image';
+import { blogPosts } from '@/data/blog';
+
+declare global {
+  interface Window {
+    __lenis?: {
+      scrollTo: (target: HTMLElement | string, options?: { offset?: number; immediate?: boolean }) => void;
+    };
+  }
+}
+
+export default function Home() {
+  const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = useState(false);
+
+  useEffect(() => {
+    if (typeof window === 'undefined') return;
+
+    const checkScreenSize = () => {
+      setIsMobile(window.innerWidth <= 768);
+    };
+
+    checkScreenSize();
+    window.addEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);
+
+    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);
+  }, []);
+
+  const handleScrollTo = (hash: string) => (event: MouseEvent<HTMLAnchorElement | HTMLButtonElement>) => {
+    if (typeof window === 'undefined') return;
+
+    event.preventDefault();
+
+    const target = document.querySelector(hash) as HTMLElement | null;
+    const lenis = window.__lenis;
+
+    if (target && lenis && typeof lenis.scrollTo === 'function') {
+      lenis.scrollTo(target, { offset: -80 });
+    } else if (target) {
+      target.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'start' });
+    }

Here’s what I implemented to turn your site into a Lenis-powered single-page experience while preserving your current look and feel.

- **Lenis smooth scrolling**
  - Added `lenis` as a dependency in `package.json:1` and created a client-side Lenis bootstrapper at `src/components/LenisScroll.tsx:1`.
  - Wired `LenisScroll` into the root layout body so it runs on every page without changing your layout to a client component (`src/app/layout.tsx:46`), and it:
    - Drives the scroll loop via `requestAnimationFrame`.
    - Stores the instance on `window.__lenis`.
    - On initial load, reads `window.location.hash` and smoothly scrolls to that section (`/#home`, `/#projects`, etc.) with an offset so it isn’t hidden behind the navbar.

- **Navbar → anchor links with smooth scroll**
  - Kept your Navigation component’s design, positions, colors, hover effects, and dark-mode toggle exactly as-is, but converted it into hash-based section navigation (`src/components/Navigation.tsx:1`):
    - Desktop nav links now point to sections:
      - `Home → /#home`
      - `Projects → /#projects`
      - `Blog → /#blog`
      - `About → /#about`
      - `Contact → /#contact` (added as a new item, matching your existing style).
    - Mobile bottom nav uses the same `/#…` targets.
  - Implemented smooth scrolling when you’re already on the home page:
    - Click handler `handleNavClick('#section')` prevents default, uses `window.__lenis.scrollTo(target, { offset: -80 })` if available, or falls back to `scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' })`.
    - Updates `window.history.pushState` so the URL hash reflects the active section without a full page reload.
  - Preserved correct highlighting:
    - Tracks `activeHash` from `window.location.hash` and listens to `hashchange`.
    - `isActive('home' | 'projects' | 'blog' | 'about' | 'contact')` uses the hash when on `/`, and `pathname` when you’re on other routes like `/blog/[slug]`.

- **Single-page layout with sections**
  - Rebuilt the home page into a single scrollable page with anchored sections while preserving your original hero and styling (`src/app/page.tsx:1`):
    - `#home` – your existing hero and “Technologies I Love” block are intact (same typography, gradients, animations, floating blobs).
      - The primary CTA buttons now scroll instead of routing:
        - “View My Work” → `/#projects` with Lenis scroll.
        - “About Me” → `/#about` with Lenis scroll.
    - `#projects` – a featured “Dictionary App” project section:
      - Styled to match your existing cards: gradient label, big title, descriptive text, key-feature chips, and device mockups using `next/image`.
      - Includes a GitHub button and a “Live Demo (Coming Soon)” button.
      - A “More projects coming soon” card plus a “View detailed project page” link that goes to `/projects` (so your full projects page is still accessible directly).
    - `#blog` – a blog summary section:

      - Each card links to the full post at `/blog/[slug]`.

    - `#about` – an about section:

  - With the new Lenis bootstrap and section IDs, these work as requested:

    const checkScreenSize = () => {
      setIsMobile(window.innerWidth <= 768);
    };

    checkScreenSize();
    window.addEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);

    return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);

  --text-primary: #f9fafb;
  --bg-secondary: #111111;
  --text-secondary: #d1d5db;
  --border-color: #333333;
  --accent-primary: #3b82f6;
  --accent-secondary: #8b5cf6;
  --background: var(--bg-primary);
  --foreground: var(--text-primary);
}

body {
  background: var(--bg-primary);
  color: var(--text-primary);
  font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;
  transition: background-color 0.3s ease, color 0.3s ease;
}

* {
  transition: background-color 0.3s ease, color 0.3s ease;
}

/* Floating animation for gradient elements */
@keyframes float {

  0%,
  100% {
    transform: translateY(0px);
  }

  50% {
    transform: translateY(-20px);
  }
}

Use this grid-based background for the whole page.

**1. Body / main wrapper**

```html
<body class="min-h-screen bg-[#1a1410] dark:bg-[#0b0b0b] text-neutral-100 antialiased overflow-hidden relative grid-bg">
```

**2. Grid background utility (add to your global CSS, e.g. `globals.css`)**

```css
@layer utilities {
  .grid-bg::before {
    content: "";
    position: fixed;
    inset: 0;
    pointer-events: none;
    opacity: 0.2;
    background-image:
      linear-gradient(to right, rgba(255,255,255,0.06) 1px, transparent 1px),
      linear-gradient(to bottom, rgba(255,255,255,0.06) 1px, transparent 1px);
    background-size: 32px 32px;
    mix-blend-mode: soft-light;
    z-index: -1;
  }
}
```

This gives you a dark brown / near-black base with thin, evenly spaced grid lines that feel technical and clean, and it works in both light and dark modes.

        }

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

}) {

+'use client';
+
+import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
+
+export default function BlogLayoutClient({
+    children,
+}: {
+    children: React.ReactNode;
+}) {
+    const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = useState(false);
+
+    useEffect(() => {
+        if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
+            const checkScreenSize = () => {
+                setIsMobile(window.innerWidth <= 768);
+            };
+
+            checkScreenSize();
+            window.addEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);
+
+            return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', checkScreenSize);

  - The grid panel is now a centered rounded rectangle at the top of the home page, not full-width and not used on any other sections.

          style={{

          }}

        </div>
      </main>

- **Grid panel styling (dark + light mode)**  
  In `src/app/globals.css`:

  ```css
  @layer utilities {
    .hero-grid {
      position: relative;
      overflow: hidden;
    }

    .hero-grid::before {
      content: "";
      position: absolute;
      top: 0;
      left: 50%;
      transform: translateX(-50%);
      width: min(1200px, 100%);
      height: 520px;
      pointer-events: none;
      border-radius: 32px;
      background-color: #f5ede6; /* light mode base */
      background-image:
        radial-gradient(circle at top, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08) 0, transparent 55%),
        radial-gradient(circle at bottom, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25) 0, transparent 60%),
        repeating-linear-gradient(
          0deg,
          #d2b39a 0px,
          #d2b39a 1px,
          transparent 1px,
          transparent 4px
        ),
        repeating-linear-gradient(
          90deg,
          #d2b39a 0px,
          #d2b39a 1px,
          transparent 1px,
          transparent 4px
        );
      z-index: 0;
    }

    .dark .hero-grid::before {
      background-color: #1a1410; /* dark brown base */
      background-image:
        radial-gradient(circle at top, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35) 0, transparent 55%),
        radial-gradient(circle at bottom, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.85) 0, transparent 60%),
        repeating-linear-gradient(
          0deg,
          #4a2b1a 0px,
          #4a2b1a 1px,
          transparent 1px,
          transparent 4px
        ),
        repeating-linear-gradient(
          90deg,
          #4a2b1a 0px,
          #4a2b1a 1px,
          transparent 1px,
          transparent 4px
        );
    }
  }
  ```

  - Light mode: warm beige grid panel.
  - Dark mode: deep brown grid panel, similar to the afgprogrammer hero.
  - The panel is centered and about 520px tall, so it sits behind your hero title and metrics and fades into the regular page background below.

- **Everything else unchanged**
  - Global body uses your normal `var(--bg-primary)` background.
  - Projects, Blog, About, Contact sections are untouched; they don’t get the grid.

After a hard refresh on `/` (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R), look at the very top hero area:

- You should see a rounded brown/beige grid panel centered behind your hero content.
- Your navbar and hero text/card should sit cleanly on top of it.
- Scroll down and the background returns to your standard dark layout.

If it’s still not matching your eye exactly, the next tweak would be adjusting the `height` (520px) and `border-radius` to more closely match that specific screenshot, but the structure and behavior are now aligned with what that site is doing.

Understood: you want a subtle circular-ish brown grid just behind your Home hero content (top center), fading out smoothly so there’s no harsh rectangle and it works in both light and dark modes.

I’ve implemented exactly that:

1. **Hero-only grid with soft circular fade**

   In `src/app/globals.css` the hero background is now:

   ```css
   @layer utilities {
     .hero-grid {
       position: relative;
       overflow: hidden;
     }

     .hero-grid::before {
       content: "";
       position: absolute;
       inset: 0;
       pointer-events: none;
       opacity: 0.5;
       background-image:
         /* soft circular brown glow that fades out */
         radial-gradient(circle at center, rgba(26, 20, 16, 0.9) 0, rgba(26, 20, 16, 0) 65%),
         /* thin grid lines (light mode) */
         repeating-linear-gradient(
           0deg,
           #d2b39a 0px,
           #d2b39a 1px,
           transparent 1px,
           transparent 4px
         ),
         repeating-linear-gradient(
           90deg,
           #d2b39a 0px,
           #d2b39a 1px,
           transparent 1px,
           transparent 4px
         );
       mix-blend-mode: soft-light;
       z-index: 0;
     }

     .dark .hero-grid::before {
       opacity: 0.6;
       background-image:
         /* stronger dark brown glow in dark mode */
         radial-gradient(circle at center, rgba(26, 20, 16, 0.95) 0, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) 68%),
         /* thin grid lines (dark mode) */
         repeating-linear-gradient(
           0deg,
           #4a2b1a 0px,
           #4a2b1a 1px,
           transparent 1px,
           transparent 4px
         ),
         repeating-linear-gradient(
           90deg,
           #4a2b1a 0px,
           #4a2b1a 1px,
           transparent 1px,
           transparent 4px
         );
     }
   }
   ```

   - The **radial-gradient** creates a circular/elliptical brown glow under the hero, fading smoothly to transparent so it doesn’t look like a hard rectangle.
   - The **repeating-linear-gradient** layers add the subtle tech grid.
   - `mix-blend-mode: soft-light` keeps it soft and non-intrusive on both light and dark backgrounds.

2. **Applied only to the Home hero**

   In `src/app/page.tsx`:

   ```tsx
   {/* Home / Hero */}
   <section id="home" className="hero-grid">
     <main style={{
       flex: 1,
       padding: '2rem 1.5rem',
       paddingTop: '6rem',
       display: 'flex',
       alignItems: 'center',
       justifyContent: 'center',
       minHeight: 'calc(100vh - 200px)'
     }}>
       <div
         style={{
           position: 'relative',
           zIndex: 1,
           textAlign: 'center',
           maxWidth: '800px',
           width: '100%'
         }}
       >
         {/* Nabi Rahmani + buttons + technologies I love */}
       </div>
     </main>
   </section>
   ```

   - `hero-grid` is only used on this `<section>`—Projects, Blog, About, Contact do not use it.
   - The inner `<div>` is `zIndex: 1`, so your hero typography, buttons, and tech badges sit cleanly above the glow and grid.

3. **Global background unchanged**

   - Your root `<div>` on the page still has `backgroundColor: 'var(--bg-primary)'`, so the overall page remains your existing dark/light background.
   - The circular grid/glow is just an overlay inside the hero.

After a hard refresh on `/` (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R), look at the hero area:

- Background is mostly your normal black/dark.
- Behind “Nabi Rahmani” and the buttons, you should see a soft brown circular glow with a subtle grid pattern, fading gently so it doesn’t form a sharp box—matching the UX you described.

If it still feels too strong or too weak, we can nudge:

- `opacity` values (0.5 / 0.6) for more/less intensity.
- The fade radius (the `65%` / `68%` numbers) to make the glow wider or tighter.

_**Agent (gpt-5.1 2025-11-29 20:28:50Z)**_

Got it – you want the brown grid only behind the hero content, centered, with a very soft circular fade (not a hard rectangle), and it should adapt to both dark and light mode.

I’ve implemented that using your two sample images as reference.

**1. Hero-only background (top center, soft circle, grid)**

In `src/app/globals.css` I replaced the old hero CSS with this:

```css
@layer utilities {
  .hero-grid {
    position: relative;
    overflow: hidden;
  }

  .hero-grid::before {
    content: "";
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    pointer-events: none;
    opacity: 0.5;
    /* soft circular brown glow + light grid for light mode */
    background-image:
      radial-gradient(
        circle at center,
        rgba(26, 20, 16, 0.9) 0,
        rgba(26, 20, 16, 0) 65%
      ),
      repeating-linear-gradient(
        0deg,
        #d2b39a 0px,
        #d2b39a 1px,
        transparent 1px,
        transparent 4px
      ),
      repeating-linear-gradient(
        90deg,
        #d2b39a 0px,
        #d2b39a 1px,
        transparent 1px,
        transparent 4px
      );
    mix-blend-mode: soft-light;
    z-index: 0;
  }

  .dark .hero-grid::before {
    opacity: 0.6;
    /* stronger dark brown glow + darker grid in dark mode */
    background-image:
      radial-gradient(
        circle at center,
        rgba(26, 20, 16, 0.95) 0,
        rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) 68%
      ),
      repeating-linear-gradient(
        0deg,
        #4a2b1a 0px,
        #4a2b1a 1px,
        transparent 1px,
        transparent 4px
      ),
      repeating-linear-gradient(
        90deg,
        #4a2b1a 0px,
        #4a2b1a 1px,
        transparent 1px,
        transparent 4px
      );
  }
}
```

- The **radial-gradient** gives that circular/elliptical brown “spotlight” behind the hero, fading out smoothly (no hard rectangle).
- The **repeating-linear-gradient** adds the thin grid lines.
- `mix-blend-mode: soft-light` keeps it subtle and lets it adapt nicely over your dark/light base.

**2. Applied only to the Home hero**

In `src/app/page.tsx` your hero section is now:

```tsx
{/* Home / Hero */}
<section id="home" className="hero-grid">
  <main style={{
    flex: 1,
    padding: '2rem 1.5rem',
    paddingTop: '6rem',
    display: 'flex',
    alignItems: 'center',
    justifyContent: 'center',
    minHeight: 'calc(100vh - 200px)'
  }}>
    <div
      style={{
        position: 'relative',
        zIndex: 1,
        textAlign: 'center',
        maxWidth: '800px',
        width: '100%'
      }}
    >
      {/* existing Nabi Rahmani hero content */}
    </div>
  </main>
</section>
```

- `hero-grid` only wraps the Home hero, so Projects/Blog/About/Contact remain clean.
- The inner `<div>` has `zIndex: 1` so your text/buttons stay on top of the glow and grid.

**3. Global background stays your current UX**

- Body/background outside the hero is still `var(--bg-primary)` (black in dark mode), so you keep your clean, dark canvas.
- The brown grid only appears under the hero content (like in your afgprogrammer screenshot), and it fades gently so it doesn’t suddenly “drop off” in color.

After a **hard refresh** on `/` (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R):

- Look only at the hero area around “Nabi Rahmani” and the buttons.
- You should now see a soft brown circular glow with a subtle grid just under that area, fading into the pure dark background—no obvious rectangle edges.

If you want the grid lines stronger or weaker, we can tweak just these two knobs:

- For stronger grid: increase `opacity` (e.g. 0.7) or use slightly brighter colors instead of `#4a2b1a`.
- For softer: lower `opacity` or increase the fade radius (`65%` / `68%` → `75%` / `80%`).

_**Agent (gpt-5.1 2025-11-29 20:45:50Z)**_

Now light mode behaves like dark mode in terms of focus: the orange grid is strongest around the hero area and much harder to see at the corners and bottom, while keeping the hero background white.

Here’s what light mode does now (`src/app/globals.css`):

```css
.hero-grid::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
  opacity: 0.6;
  /* Light mode: pure white base, orange grid strongest near center, faint at edges */
  background-color: transparent;
  background-image:
    /* 1. Bottom fade – grid becomes very subtle toward the bottom of Home */
    linear-gradient(
      to bottom,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0) 0%,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9) 100%
    ),
    /* 2. Vignette – corners lighten so grid is hard to see there */
    radial-gradient(
      circle at center,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0) 0,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9) 80%
    ),
    /* 3. Orange grid overlay */
    repeating-linear-gradient(
      0deg,
      rgba(255, 107, 53, 0.4) 0px,
      rgba(255, 107, 53, 0.4) 1px,
      transparent 1px,
      transparent 18px
    ),
    repeating-linear-gradient(
      90deg,
      rgba(255, 107, 53, 0.4) 0px,
      rgba(255, 107, 53, 0.4) 1px,
      transparent 1px,
      transparent 18px
    );
}
```

- Hero remains **white** in light mode; only an orange grid is overlaid.
- The **center/top area** shows the orange grid most clearly.
- The **corners and bottom** are brightened by the white gradients, so the grid there is “poor / hard to see,” similar to how dark mode uses dark gradients to hide the grid at the edges.

Dark mode (`.dark .hero-grid::before`) is unchanged and still uses the rich brown panel with grid.

After a hard refresh, in light mode you should see:

- A white hero with a subtle orange grid clearly around the hero content.
- The grid fading out toward the corners and bottom, not a flat, even grid everywhere.

_**Agent (gpt-5.1 2025-11-29 20:51:54Z)**_

You’re right: on mobile the theme switcher was getting cramped because the bottom nav had a fixed narrow width and each item had a fairly large minimum width.

I’ve adjusted the mobile nav so everything fits cleanly, and the theme switcher is fully visible:

**Changes in `src/components/Navigation.tsx` (mobile bottom nav only):**

- **Nav container width made responsive and slightly wider:**

  ```ts
  {isMobile && (
    <nav
      style={{
        position: 'fixed',
        bottom: '1.5rem',
        left: '50%',
        transform: 'translateX(-50%)',
        zIndex: 50,
        backgroundColor: `${isDark ? 'rgba(0,0,0,0.9)' : 'rgba(255,255,255,0.9)'}`,
        backdropFilter: 'blur(16px)',
        border: `1px solid var(--border-color)`,
        borderRadius: '2rem',
        padding: '0.75rem 1rem',
        transition: 'all 0.3s ease',
        boxShadow: isDark
          ? '0 8px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.3)'
          : '0 8px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)',
        width: '90%',          // was 'auto'
        minWidth: '260px',     // was 300
        maxWidth: '380px',     // was 350
      }}
    >
  ```

- **Each mobile item (Home / Projects / Blog / About / Contact / Theme) now has a smaller min width:**

  ```ts
  // Example for Home link
  <Link
    href="/"
    style={{
      display: 'flex',
      flexDirection: 'column',
      alignItems: 'center',
      gap: '0.25rem',
      color: isActive('home') ? 'rgba(252, 180, 176, 1)' : 'var(--text-secondary)',
      textDecoration: 'none',
      padding: '0.5rem',
      borderRadius: '0.75rem',
      backgroundColor: isActive('home') ? 'rgba(252, 180, 176, 0.1)' : 'transparent',
      transition: 'all 0.3s ease',
      minWidth: '48px',       // was 60px
    }}
    onClick={handleNavClick('#home')}
  >
  ```

  - The same `minWidth: '48px'` change is applied to Projects, Blog, About, Contact, and the Theme button.

This combination means:

- The nav bar can grow up to ~380px or shrink down to 260px / 90% of the viewport.
- Each icon+label block uses less minimum width.
- All six items now fit within the nav without clipping, so the theme switcher is no longer half outside on mobile.

After a hard refresh and switching to a mobile viewport, you should see the bottom nav with all icons, labels, and the Theme switcher fully visible and centered.
